articles.title: US Navy, Gecko Robotics surge AI maintenance contract to $300M
articles.snippet: Gecko Robotics uses drones, wall-climbing robots and fixed sensors to gather data on components, decks, welds and hulls.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Navy is ramping up its investment in artificial intelligence technology to streamline ship repairs and resolve maintenance logjams.
Gecko Robotics announced Tuesday that the Navy is increasing the value of its initial contract to up to $300 million — just six months after the company reached an initial agreement with the sea service.
“Gecko’s AI and robotic technology can save the U.S. Navy up to $8 million in repair costs per ship and return vessels to sea quicker by identifying structural issues up to 50 times faster than traditional methods — reducing inspections from months to days,” Gecko Robotics said in a release.
The initial contract began as a 5-year, $54 million indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity deal for Gecko to work on 18 ships assigned to the Navy’s U.S. Pacific Fleet.
The company uses drones, wall-climbing robots and fixed sensors to gather data on components, decks, welds and hulls.
That information, paired with AI tools, is used to identify current and potential structural issues that may remain hidden to the naked eye.
A key part of the new contract investment is Gecko Robotics’ Komodo machine system, which analyzes the health of deck coatings by scanning — eliminating the need to physically dig into them.
This allows the Navy to plan repairs and map out damaged areas before the ship enters dry dock, something that previously only occurred after the maintenance cycle began.
The Navy has consistently stated its goal of reaching 80% fleet readiness by 2027, despite criticisms of the service’s deployment capabilities.
The Government Accountability Office reported in December 2024 that readiness rates among the Navy’s amphibious warfare ships fell to 46% between 2011 and 2020, hindering Marine Corps deployment and training plans.
In August 2025, that rate reportedly dipped to just 41%, resulting in a more than five-month gap in Marine Expeditionary Unit deployments that year and further straining resources amid the Trump administration’s push to counter the illicit drug trade in Latin America and the Caribbean.
Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle, who adopted the 80% goal from his predecessor Adm. Lisa Franchetti, laid out the major tenets for achieving the ambitious milestone.
“Achieving this requires shorter maintenance cycles, increased spare-parts availability, improved training pipelines and targeted upgrades across the fleet,” Caudle wrote for Military Times in December.
Riley Ceder is a Navy reporter at Military Times, where he covers issues directly affecting service members and their families, as well as breaking news.
J.D. Simkins is Editor-in-Chief of Military Times and Defense News, and a Marine Corps veteran of the Iraq War.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy says US decisions on Ukraine hard to explain
articles.snippet: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy laments delayed arms shipments, saying the Trump administration is dragging its feet.
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that decisions taken by the United States on the war in Ukraine, including delays in arms shipments and restrictions on intelligence sharing, were “hard to explain.”
“Because it all comes down to (Russian President Vladimir) Putin’s refusal to end this war, and to decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends,” Zelenskyy said in a meeting with a U.S. congressional delegation.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had not received full explanations over limitations placed on the use of the Starshield system needed to stage some drone strikes and defend against Russian attacks, particularly by high-speed jet-powered drones.
In remarks posted on a video on Telegram, he said that on three occasions in the past week, Ukraine had not received the advance warning of an attack generally provided by its partners.
“We also know that, unfortunately, the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that our partner have already paid for through the PURL programme,” he said.
He said that to his knowledge one missile package was waiting for signature by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
“All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us,” he said.
Affected by the U.S. delays are urgently needed Patriot interceptor missiles, just as Russia has intensified its targeting of Ukrainian cities with missiles and drones, the Washington Post reported.
Zelenskyy also said that Ukraine was willing to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, as demanded by U.S. President Donald Trump, for 30 days if Washington supplied Ukraine with interceptors for the Patriot anti-missile system.
He also said that he hoped a Ukrainian delegation would meet in the coming days with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Norway.

articles.title: Tip of the spear, or stranded on beaches? Chinese planners dissect USMC Pacific posture
articles.snippet: Understanding these dynamics, American leaders should recalibrate and opt to rely less on forward defense, writes analyst Lyle Goldstein.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Navy has taken some heat recently for focusing too heavily on the Middle East and neglecting the Asia-Pacific. The same cannot be said of the U.S. Marine Corps, which unveiled a new strategy in 2019 relying on dispersed groups of Marines to wield drones and anti-ship missiles in archipelagic warfare in order to unhinge Chinese maritime expansion. As the Marines are developing new capabilities at the pointy end of the American spear, so to speak, it’s not surprising that USMC strategy is attracting lots of attention from Chinese defense experts. This article summarizes several recent Chinese-language assessments.
The close attention that Beijing is paying to the new USMC strategy became clear about a year ago when the Global Times [环球时报] published an unusual editorial decrying Washington’s new determination to deploy anti-ship missiles proximate to China. Arguing that the new American strategy aims to correct a U.S. Navy prioritization for “open ocean control” rather than “close-quarters engagement in confined waters,” this article concludes that Washington’s effort to “control maritime chokepoints [aims to] curtail the freedom of rivals to operate at sea … [and] introduces new risks … .”
A much more detailed study of the new USMC strategy appeared in early 2025 in the naval magazine Modern Ships [现代舰船]. This Chinese assessment noted with considerable alarm that the USMC was experimenting with unmanned surface vessels capable of firing the stealthy LRASM anti-ship cruise missile and that these units could alternatively serve as forward scouts, fixing targets for long-range U.S. military fires. Still, this analysis underlines some weaknesses of the USMC strategy, including the range limitations of related sensors and drones, and even characterized the air-defense capabilities of the USMC as “precarious.” Another study in this same magazine had earlier drawn attention to the logistics quandaries raised by the new strategy.
A 2026 Chinese analysis in another Chinese navy-affiliated magazine, Shipborne Weapons [舰载武器], offers a sharper critique of the Marines’ new approach, noting that the creation of the Marine Littoral Regiments (MLR) “actually represents campaign preparation by the USMC to militarily intervene in China’s unification.” At the outset, this study notes that many American think tanks raised doubts about the strategy, suggesting that forward bases without sea and air control could prove “untenable.”
There is a recognition in this analysis that the new mobile missile launchers that are being deployed by the USMC are small, light, and thus “not easily discovered by … surveillance.” In the end, this study concludes that the USMC strategy is vulnerable because the “U.S has no way to quickly establish air superiority. This could take weeks or months and would entail massive losses.”
Among the most remarkable pieces written by Chinese experts on the new USMC direction is one that was published in translation recently by the China institute at U.S. Naval War College (NWC). That translation deserves extra attention due to the fact that it was written by senior active-duty Chinese Navy officers and also because it was published originally in a sensitive internal circulation Chinese military journal too.
Though this piece does not touch directly on the sensitive Taiwan issue, and it also explicitly notes the USMC strategy aims at deterrence of Beijing, it nevertheless explains that the new USMC deployments amount to “continuous penetration and encroachment into our near seas” and argues that China must “establish effective countermeasures.” Notably, this high-level rendering links the USMC strategy to China’s improving submarine force in significant detail, observing that forward deployed Marine forces could deploy “hydro-acoustic arrays and other assets to establish barrier zones and monitoring areas to track Chinese submarine operations.” Similar arguments are made that U.S. deployments could degrade Chinese air defenses by employing drone swarms “to overwhelm our radar tracking capacity.”
The Chinese Navy authors caution against applying resource-intensive assets to defeat such American asymmetric tactics. However, the conclusion of the article is rather disturbing since it argues that China must counter this posture by deploying a Chinese “proactive offensive posture, aggressively expand[ing] our operational reach, [and] project[ing] forces forward.” Elaborating, they counsel: “We must maintain and normalize forward-deployed forces, extend[ing] undersea combat capabilities as far forward as feasible.”
This conclusion and other aspects of these Chinese-language analyses raise some rather uncomfortable questions for U.S. defense planners. The final translation done by NWC strongly hints that the Chinese Navy may be adopting a more aggressive approach as a direct reaction to the forward lean in American strategy. This seems to be a very clear manifestation of the so-called ‘security dilemma,’ wherein two powers’ defensive measures develop into a dangerous escalatory spiral. Moreover, there is a clear recognition by Chinese strategists that forward USMC elements could be vulnerable due to logistics challenges and lack of proper air and missile defenses. It would not be the first time that the USMC was deployed haphazardly in East Asia at the cost of many American lives.
Understanding these dynamics, American leaders should recalibrate and opt to rely less on forward defense. Alternatively, the USMC should aim to embrace the strategic depth of the Pacific and its myriad island archipelagos (e.g. the Philippines) in a less costly, less risky, more sustainable, and clearly defensive strategy.
Lyle Goldstein is director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School and concurrently serves as director of the Asia Program at the think-tank Defense Priorities.

articles.title: Pentagon, BAE sign deal for up to 25,000 precision-guided munition kits a year
articles.snippet: The Pentagon and BAE Systems signed a framework agreement for up to 25,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, or APKWS, guidance kits a year.
articles.full_text:
The Defense Department has signed a framework agreement with BAE Systems to buy up to 25,000 Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System, or APKWS, guidance kits a year for as long as seven years, the department announced Monday.
APKWS kits convert unguided 2.75-inch rockets into laser-guided munitions. All four services field them, and the weapon has become a cheaper alternative to air-to-air missiles for shooting down drones.
Congress still has to approve and fund the buy, the department said. BAE said it will increase production while the two sides work out a multiyear contract. Neither side announced the deal’s cost.
The framework also outlines a path to increase output to 35,000 kits a year for U.S. allies. The department said that added capacity will come online as partner nations formally request kits through the Foreign Military Sales program.
“By securing multi-year demand, this agreement keeps production lines running at capacity, provides our forces with interceptor inventory, and flips the cost calculus in the taxpayer’s favor,” Michael Duffey, the Pentagon’s undersecretary for acquisition and sustainment, said in the announcement.
BAE, which builds the kits in Hudson, New Hampshire, and Austin, Texas, said in February that it had delivered its 100,000th kit.
The 25,000 figure in this framework agreement matches capacity BAE has cited before. A company official said in 2023 that APKWS was in full-rate production with room to grow to 25,000 units a year.
“APKWS delivers proven, reliable and affordable precision at scale to counter evolving threats and ensure our warfighters maintain a decisive advantage,” said Tom Arseneault, president and CEO of BAE Systems Inc.
The Navy’s current five-year APKWS contract with BAE, awarded in August 2025, is worth up to $1.74 billion. It covers up to 55,000 kits for the Navy, the Army and foreign customers, with work expected to be completed by December 2031.
Among allied buyers, Saudi Arabia won State Department approval in July for a possible $1.96 billion package that includes up to 20,000 APKWS kits, split evenly between air-to-air and air-to-ground versions. Italy is also weighing a buy of 5,031 kits for counter-drone defense.
The APKWS agreement is the latest in a series of framework deals the Pentagon has signed this year to boost munitions production.
In January, Lockheed Martin agreed to more than triple production of the Patriot Advanced Capability-3 Missile Segment Enhancement, or PAC-3 MSE, interceptor.
In March, BAE and Lockheed agreed to quadruple production of seekers for the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, interceptor. A separate THAAD framework signed in January led to a June contract worth more than $35 billion for the interceptors themselves.
Michael Scanlon is a defense journalist covering air and space warfare. A former U.S. Air Force A-10 crew chief, he has supported land and sea programs for the U.S. Army, Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.

articles.title: US Army competition explores military uses for humanoid robots
articles.snippet: They're still a long way off from mass-producing Terminators.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Army’s program for accelerating new technologies announced the winners of a humanoid robot competition, which assessed how the emerging technology could contribute to future military operations.
According to the Sept. 29 announcement, the five winners of the Army’s xTechHumanoid competition include ACES Group, IHMC Robotics, Hydroplane Limited, Ras Labs and Velocity Explorations.
Alex Miller, the Army’s chief technology officer, explained that through the program, the service tried to identify “the problems, mission needs, and opportunities” humanoid robots could best be used.
“xTech is our method of surveying the industry landscape and fast-tracking promising technology rather than falling victim to years-long studies,” Miller said.
“Humanoid robots are part of a broader autonomy push to increase the depth and breadth of robotic platforms and components industry can provide for a range of missions,” he added.
The expectation
For the competition, Army officials reviewed each company’s white paper proposal for its humanoid robot. They evaluated the concepts based on several criteria, including military utility, technical merit and technological maturity.
Of the 103 submissions, the Army selected 10 finalists, each of which received $25,000. The service then identified five winners through a live experimentation event.
According to the 2025 competition announcement, the event tested the robots on a series of collective tasks “in the context of a military small unit mission conducted in a combat situation.”
During the event, officials also reviewed the baseline system capabilities and advanced subsystems.
Examples of the former include checkpoint security, gap crossing or obstacle clearing and firefighting. Whereas the latter included technologies like thermal sensors, battery life and autonomy.
The reality
However, Robert Griffin, a senior researcher at IHMC Robotics, told Military Times that the competition’s individual requirements exceeded what current technology could achieve.
“The individual things that were outlined were, in any one element, beyond what is possible given the current state of the art,” Griffin said.
“For example, you don’t have a robot that can run 28 miles an hour while carrying 50 pounds and operating for 24 hours,” he said. “It’s not a thing that exists in the world.”
Because the Army’s “actual full desirements were beyond what can currently be done,” Griffin said, developers had to prioritize different elements of their robots’ capabilities for the demonstrations.
Griffin’s team focused on baseline capabilities.
“The big thing for us was to have the robot show up at the competition, move around in the world, unsupported, at a reasonable pace, and then respond to commands,” he said.
Video of the competition shows IHMC’s robot “Alex” following voice commands directing it to walk through a field and then, under the control of a human with a remote, through the woods and across gravel.
Alex also grasps a small shovel, begins to dig and attempts to pour dirt into a bucket. Although it doesn’t succeed, it demonstrates the movement. And finally, Alex collapses and has to be transported out on a gurney.
Testing subsystems
Other competitors focused on subsystems.
Hydroplane and ACES Group competed with their batteries, while Velocity Explorations entered software that enabled its robot to listen to radio traffic between people and understand their movements and tasks. Using that information to develop an understanding of the broader battlespace, the platform could then determine how to act.
Ras Labs tested highly sensitive fingertip tactile sensors that allowed a robot to handle delicate objects.
While multiple companies said they participated because it was a chance to test their products, Dr. Anita Sengupta, Hydroplane’s founder and chief executive, explained that her company has traditionally done work for large structures and aircraft, but recently started working on smaller and portable systems.
“We saw a good overlap between developing a power system for a humanoid, whether it’s a person or a robot, as well as the drone use case, so it just seemed like an interesting use case for us to take our technology to,” she said.
For the competition, her company adapted a 10-kilowatt system originally designed for the Marine Corps in 2024, but made it smaller because the humanoid only needed a few kilowatts. The device utilizes a fuel cell similar to what a generator uses, but instead of using diesel fuel, it uses hydrogen. Sengupta explained that the benefits are that it has about three times the energy density and a higher conversion efficiency.
Although Hydroplane didn’t directly power a humanoid robot with its fuel cell, the Army tested it to see if it could power a humanoid robot. In turn, Hydroplane helped establish those standards, with the intent to eventually collaborate with a humanoid robot team.
The future
In the recent announcement, the Army said the competition revealed a clear picture of “both the progress commercial industry has made in humanoid robotics and the technical challenges that remain.” The findings, the service said, will help it direct research toward technologies that offer the greatest return for warfighters.
But while humanoid robots might eventually take on more complex military tasks, Griffin said the industry is still a long way from developing machines like Arnold Schwarzenegger’s T-800 from The Terminator franchise.
“I don’t think that any person who has a modicum of ethics is going to say that we need to be having these robots making life or death decisions,” he said, noting how easily current AI models can be confused or manipulated.
Instead, Griffin said the future of humanoid robotics will depend in part on what investors want the machines to do. Industrial companies, for example, may see opportunities to automate tasks typically performed by humans.
“Our goal is to be able to make robots that remove people from having to do harmful tasks,” he said about his company, pointing to scenarios such as first responders entering burning buildings and nuclear cleanup.
Daniel Terrill is a contributor to Military Times. He’s been reporting on military issues, the gun industry, and the outdoors for nearly two decades. Although writing is his passion, he’s been a Marine, police officer, and, perhaps the most dangerous job of his career, a substitute teacher.

articles.title: Shield AI software cuts autonomous flight development to six weeks
articles.snippet: Shield AI said this week that its Hivemind software helped Honeywell Aerospace achieve autonomous flight after six weeks, down from 54 weeks.
articles.full_text:
The California-based defense company Shield AI said this week that its Hivemind software helped Honeywell Aerospace achieve autonomous flight after six weeks of training, down from an estimated 54 weeks, ahead of two flight demonstrations, according to Monday’s joint statement.
“Hivemind Enterprise handled the autonomy basics, so [Honeywell engineers] could spend its time on its own detection and tracking model,” said Tom Schaefer, vice president of Hivemind Enterprise at Shield AI. “We built Hivemind so partners can work this way.”
The companies announced their collaboration in July along with a memorandum of understanding, stating their goal was to help “defense operators move from demonstration to deployment faster… without having to rebuild confidence in each new system every time.”
Shield AI explained the Hivemind software provides “core capabilities such as route planning, mission management, and communication between aircraft,” so companies like Honeywell could integrate “their own AI models, sensors, and mission capabilities and [advance] them from simulation to flight.”
According to the statement, Honeywell’s autonomy team began training on Hivemind in late April and by mid-June, they flew a BFD-SE8 multirotor aircraft autonomously for the first time using the newly developed autonomy stack.
The team held the official demonstration on July 8 in Plymouth, Minnesota, where the aircraft took off on its own, followed a planned route, re-routed around a no-fly zone, and returned to base.
Afterward, the company said, the team immediately began working on the second demonstration. For three months, they trained and deployed their own target detection and tracking model.
On Oct. 8, the team hosted another demonstration in which a scout aircraft used the AI model to detect, identify, and track a target. It then passed the information to another aircraft, which navigated autonomously to the target, delivered a payload, and then returned to base with the scout.
Todd Giles, Honeywell Aerospace’s senior vice president of engineering and chief technology officer, credited “open architectures” — or the use of public standards for software development — for “changing the pace of innovation in aerospace” and his team’s accomplishment.
“By combining our expertise in avionics, navigation, sensing, and autonomy, we are helping create a scalable foundation for the next generation of autonomous aircraft and mission systems,” Giles said.

articles.title: Groups seek clarity on motive behind Pentagon’s study of women in combat
articles.snippet: Citing concerns about Hegseth’s views on the topic, the lawsuit asks for records showing the scope, purpose, methodology and anticipated use of the study.
articles.full_text:
A group of civil rights organizations sued the Defense Department for records behind its decision to study women’s “effectiveness” in combat roles a decade after the military opened those positions to women.
The lawsuit, filed by the American Civil Liberties Union, or ACLU, alongside two other groups, asks a federal court to enforce their request for information about why the Pentagon commissioned the study.
In a statement, Gillian Thomas, senior counsel for the ACLU’s Women’s Rights Project, argued that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has “repeatedly, without evidence, questioned women’s ability to serve in ground combat,” aims to deliver research to validate his “biased” views.
“Now, without explanation, he has commissioned a study of women’s performance and assigned it to a researcher with a record of criticizing women’s combat readiness,” she said. “The public has a right to know why, and what he plans to do with the results.”
In January, the Defense Department commissioned a non-profit research group called the Institute for Defense Analyses, which is largely funded by the federal government, to study the topic for six months.
However, according to the lawsuit, the study was reassigned to the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, or JHU/APL, in April 2026, where the lead researcher, Jane Pinelis, authored a 2015 study for the Marine Corps that found “negative effects of mixed-gender units.”
The lawsuit adds that the 2015 study “was widely criticized for its flawed design and biased analysis.” Those critics, including the Navy Secretary at the time, described it as attempting to show that men are stronger than women rather than establish minimum standards and see who could meet them.
Additionally, The War Horse reported that Hegseth relied heavily on that study to support his argument that women shouldn’t serve in combat roles in his book The War on Warriors.
“Dads push us to take risks. Moms put the training wheels on our bikes,” he wrote in the book. “We need moms. But not in the military, especially in combat units.”
In a November 2024 interview on the Sean Ryan Podcast, Hegseth shared his explicit view on the issue: “I’m straight up just saying we should not have women in combat roles.”
Although he has since softened his rhetoric on women in combat, critics say he continues to push the agenda under the guise of military standards.
According to the lawsuit, the ACLU, the National Women’s Law Center and the Service Women’s Action Network want Defense Department records showing the scope, purpose, methodology and anticipated use of the study.

articles.title: US Army Cyber Command charts course for human-AI equilibrium
articles.snippet: U.S. Army Cyber Command is constantly refining human oversight of artificial intelligence, Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank said last week.
articles.full_text:
The head of Army Cyber Command said last week that the service was constantly observing and refining human oversight of artificial intelligence, with the possibility of releasing computer agents to do some work by themselves.
Speaking at the Association of the United States Army Conference in Washington, Lt. Gen. Christopher Eubank described an iterative human-in-the-loop process in which military personnel learn in real time how to balance giving AI agents autonomy and exercising control over them.
“It’s occurring daily and weekly inside of the headquarters as we watch agents learn and grow, and then determine what we should let them do on their own versus have a human in the loop,” Eubank said. “All work right now is safeguarded human-in-the-loop as we continue to learn across this very important emergent technology.”
Military personnel currently watch AI agents perform routine tasks, with a governance board within Army Cyber Command making decisions on whether that agent should be allowed to continue performing a task without human intervention or whether it should be allowed to work unsupervised.
During its current human-in-the-loop iteration, every machine AI team checked in with the human team daily and was not operating alone.
Every AI agent was also assigned the same work role as a human, so Army Cyber command trained those agents to be masters of their craft in the same way the Army did with the humans.
As the service worked through the iterative process, the uptick in speed that AI ushered in was drastic.
In two days, an AI agent could complete work that took an analytics support officer six months, Eubank said.
Army Cyber Command used artificial intelligence to operate, secure, defend and attack networks, and make sure that technology works hand in hand with the human workforce, according to Eubank.
Artificial intelligence also enabled the command to move faster than it had ever moved and sift through mountains of data at machine speed, which allowed humans to focus on solving critical problems.
Riley Ceder is a Navy reporter at Military Times, where he covers issues directly affecting service members and their families, as well as breaking news.

articles.title: Russian satellite stalked ICEYE spacecraft in potentially dangerous on-orbit maneuvers
articles.snippet: The Cosmos 2612 came within 500 meters (about a third of a mile) to US-flagged ICEYE-X36 believed to be supporting Ukraine, according to LeoLabs.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — In an unprecedented move, A Russian government-owned satellite spent weeks stalking an ICEYE satellite widely believed to be providing synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery to Ukraine — coming as close as 500 meters (about a third of a mile), according to space watching firm LeoLabs.
In a press release today, LeoLabs said Russia’s Cosmos 2612 “conducted a deliberate series of maneuvers toward ICEYE-X36” between Oct. 15-19 that involved “continued maneuvering around ICEYE-X36, shifting between positions ahead of and behind the commercial satellite.”
While Russia’s Cosmos birds have previously been observed closely following other Western satellites, Adam Marsh, LeoLabs vice president for technical solutions, told Breaking Defense that this was a first-of-its-kind rendezvous and proximity operation (RPO).
“This is the most advanced and potentially dangerous uncooperative RPO we’ve observed,” he said.
Victoria Samson, chief director of Space Security and Stability for Secure World Foundation, agreed.
“What is new is that I don’t think that there has ever been an uncoordinated RPO that was close,” she told Breaking Defense. “Also, in these earlier cases, the satellite that was being approached was a USG satellite; obviously in this case, it was a commercial satellite.”
LeoLabs’ analysis concluded that Cosmos 2612 “demonstrated a sequence of capabilities that could be used to inspect, characterize, shadow, or potentially interfere with another spacecraft. The observed tactics included:
- Departing on a controlled trajectory
- Deliberately matching the orbital plane of another satellite
- Closing from long range in a controlled manner
- Adjusting speed and altitude to manage relative motion
- Repositioning ahead of and behind the target
- Remaining close rather than conducting a simple flyby
- Making repeated small maneuvers while in proximity.”
According to a blog post by longtime space watcher Marco Langbroek, the Cosmos 2612 ― which was launched in April ― began its “worrisome” stalking mission Sept. 30 and subsequently undertook a series of maneuvers “clearly designed” to catch up to the ICEYE satellite.
Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said in a web post on Friday that Cosmos 2612’s maneuvers should be viewed as a likely threat, given that the ICEYE satellite “supports Ukraine” in its effort to repel Russia’s 2022 invasion.
(ICEYE, however, has not publicly confirmed the customer(s) for ICEYE-X36.)
“Given Russia’s history of testing on-orbit weapons, policymakers should assume Cosmos 2612 could take an action that threatens the commercial satellite,” he wrote. “But the risk extends beyond just one satellite. A Russian counterspace activity in the vicinity of Western satellites should be assessed within the context of aggressive Russian gray zone activities targeting U.S. and European interests.”
ICEYE, headquartered in Finland, first announced an agreement with Ukraine to provide SAR imagery via a dedicated satellite in 2022, but has never publicly identified which specific satellite was provided.
Samson noted that although ICEYE-X36 may be collecting data used by Ukraine, the spacecraft is operated by its US arm, ICEYE US, and was launched from the United States in 2024. That makes ICEYE-X36 a US satellite — or at least one for which the United States is the launching state, she explained.
“Russia and the US aren’t at war with each other, knock wood, but this does make me wonder why the USG [US government] has been silent on this matter,” she added.

articles.title: EU cyber law won’t force fixes for fridge controllers hit in French attack
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The EU’s Cyber Resilience Act that took effect last month only requires companies to fix vulnerabilities and issue free updates during a product's support period, which manufacturers define.
articles.full_text:
EU cyber law won’t force fixes for fridge controllers hit in French attack
The European Union’s new cyber rules require manufacturers to report attacks exploiting their end-of-life products, but does not force them to fix the issues, the bloc’s cybersecurity agency said Monday, after a cyberattack hit hundreds of French supermarkets’ refrigeration systems.
Earlier this month, hackers compromised internet-exposed remote controllers for refrigeration systems at numerous French supermarkets, forcing some units into a continuous defrost cycle at 50°C, according to reports at the time.
Grocery chains including Intermarché, Carrefour, Monoprix, Leclerc and Coopérative U were affected, with monetary losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros as spoiled food stock had to be thrown away.
France’s cybersecurity agency ANSSI said it was “aware of the compromise of refrigeration system remote controllers,” naming Danfoss’s AK-SM and AK-SC series, Copeland’s xweb and Dixell’s xweb products.
The agency’s emergency response team, CERT-FR, issued an alert last Monday and ANSSI urged operators to disconnect or filter any controllers exposed to the internet to prevent further attacks.
“Investigations are on-going,” the agency told Recorded Future News, adding that it was coordinating preventive and remediation measures across sectors that might be affected, “with a specific focus on mass retailers.”
In a statement, Copeland acknowledged “the vulnerability identified in a discontinued, end-of-life generation of controllers,” adding it was “currently working with impacted customers to mitigate the risk.”
The company said it would “continue to support customers in strengthening cybersecurity through supported products, current software and industry-recommended practices.” It did not say how many customers were affected.
Danfoss did not respond to a request for comment, but has said its affected units were also end-of-life.
The Paris prosecutor’s office told Recorded Future News it had received “about ten complaints” and estimated the “number of victims at around 700.” Its investigation is also ongoing, and it said that to date no perpetrator has claimed responsibility for the attack.
EU response
Provisions of the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act that took effect last month require manufacturers of connected hardware and software devices sold in the bloc — from consumer gadgets to industrial controllers like those hit in France — to report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents affecting their products.
ENISA — the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity — told Recorded Future News that the obligation covers end-of-life products “no longer sold in the EU, but which remain in use,” and that “the reporting obligations continue to apply after a product with digital elements is no longer supported.”
However the law’s separate obligations to handle vulnerabilities, including fixing them and issuing free security updates, apply only during a product’s support period, which manufacturers define.
Where a product was placed on the market before December 11, 2027, or its support has ended — as in the fridge controllers targeted in this instance — “the manufacturer is not required to comply with the vulnerability handling obligations,” said ENISA.
The agency declined to share information on specific notices it may have received from manufacturers and would not say whether any had reported the attacks. It said the EU CSIRTs Network of national cyber emergency response teams “is actively exchanging info and monitoring the situation.”
ANSSI added it was also “equally mobilized at the European level and is maintaining regular dialogue with its counterparts.”
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: AOMEI yet to notify customers after hackers hijacked its software updates
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: In an email, the Hong Kong-registered company confirmed to Recorded Future News that hackers repeatedly altered configuration files on its update servers between April and July, redirecting the software to download malware for minutes at a time.
articles.full_text:
AOMEI yet to notify customers after hackers hijacked its software updates
AOMEI, the maker of a standalone Windows backup tool, said Tuesday it has not yet identified or notified customers who were infected with malware after hackers hijacked its update server in a monthslong supply-chain attack.
In an email, the Hong Kong-registered company confirmed to Recorded Future News that hackers repeatedly altered configuration files on its update servers between April and July, redirecting the software to download malware for minutes at a time.
The confirmation follows coordinated reports published last week by cybersecurity firm ManageEngine, whose researchers first detected the activity, and Google Threat Intelligence Group which investigated it further.
Google’s researchers said it was the first time they had encountered a supply-chain compromise with such short-burst tampering windows, “effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning.”
ManageEngine said it first warned AOMEI in June, after its software detected suspicious activity at two customers. According to ManageEngine, AOMEI initially blamed malicious actors intercepting and modifying its update in transit rather than any issue on its own end.
The attackers struck at least twice more after the first warning, when AOMEI said it investigated the incident and “rectified some potential vulnerabilities,” but was “unable to pinpoint the root cause” of the breach during that investigation.
AOMEI added that it was only after ManageEngine’s report in July, when the researchers provided “the specific time at which the tampering occurred,” that its team was able to identify “traces of the intrusion” by analysing server logs and comparing files. It said it then updated the server and has found no traces of malicious files since.
AOMEI did not address ManageEngine’s account of its initial explanation. The company claimed that Google and ManageEngine had since told it the issue was resolved, although ManageEngine’s report states it had not independently verified that the attackers had lost access to AOMEI’s infrastructure.
Google said it had notified the victims that it had identified, saying they spanned IT services, telecommunications and higher education in almost a dozen countries including the U.S., Australia, India and Brazil.
However the Google researchers warned that because the malware was sent to anyone who checked for updates during the attack windows, the true number of victims is probably higher: “Given the short duration of these windows, it is probable that additional tampering occurred throughout the campaign that remained outside our visibility.”
They are tracking the threat cluster as UNC7017.
“Nothing in AOMEI Backupper was exploited,” ManageEngine wrote. The attackers instead abused the channel AOMEI uses to deliver promotional pop-ups, which didn’t authenticate the configuration files. After each tampering window, the attackers restored the original files, leaving nothing for later inspections to find.
“A backup tool runs constantly, reaches every file on the machine, is trusted by the people who installed it, and talks to its vendor on a schedule, so nothing it does looks out of place,” the ManageEngine researchers told Recorded Future News. “For an operator who wants to go unnoticed, a backup vendor’s update channel is close to perfect cover.”
During the July 20 window, Google said, the attackers also used an invisible pop-up to coerce machines into sending Windows password hashes to an attacker-controlled server, a technique that could work even where the malware itself was blocked.
Both Google and ManageEngine warned that AOMEI’s server fixes would not clean computers that had already been infected, and urged organizations using AOMEI software to hunt for signs of compromise across the whole April–July period.
ManageEngine said Google’s report also documents targeting of AnyViewer, AOMEI’s remote-desktop product although AOMEI said its monitoring found that “only AOMEI Backupper exhibited anomalies,” with “no abnormal activity” in AnyViewer.
UNC7017’s origin and motivation remains unknown. According to ManageEngine, the malware used by the group was designed to stop if a computer appeared to be in China, if its location could not be determined or if certain security products were installed.
“This campaign was built to leave no trace, and that includes its identity,” the researchers said. They cautioned that the China exclusion did not establish where the attackers were based, and could be intended to avoid local law enforcement, avoid particular security firms or mislead investigators.
AOMEI said the company “will assess potentially affected users, proactively connect them, and work with them to implement the necessary security measures.”
The company has released a free detection tool and is urging anyone who used Backupper during the exposure windows to update and scan their systems.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Anti-Putin messages disrupt nationwide school assessments in Russia
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A pro-Ukraine group that says it operates within Russia took responsibility for anti-Putin messages appearing on an education assessment platform. Authorities said they had restored systems.
articles.full_text:
Anti-Putin messages disrupt nationwide school assessments in Russia
Russia's education watchdog says it has restored its online systems following a cyberattack that disrupted nationwide school assessments and displayed messages urging students to join an underground movement against President Vladimir Putin.
The attack last Friday forced Rosobrnadzor to suspend assessments at schools and vocational education institutions across the country. Students completing questionnaires on the agency's Edutest platform were shown anti-government messages instead of questions, according to Russian officials.
Rosobrnadzor said on Monday the attacks targeted its online resources and those of the Federal Institute for Education Quality Assessment (FIOKO), a subordinate organization responsible for assessing education standards.
A pro-Ukrainian hacking group calling itself Black Spark claimed responsibility for the disruption. The group describes itself as an underground resistance movement operating inside Russia and has previously claimed responsibility for attacks against Russian technology companies.
Ekaterina Mizulina, a controversial pro-Kremlin activist who heads Russia's Safe Internet League, said she had received reports from students at schools across the Moscow region who encountered the messages while taking the assessments.
"Halfway through the assessment, when they moved on to another question, the same image appeared on everyone's screens, urging them to take part in anti-government activities," Mizulina wrote, sharing a photograph that appeared to show the message on school computers.
The disruption coincided with a major stage of the nationwide assessment program, during which 9th grade students in 29 Russian regions were scheduled to complete questionnaires, according to local media reports.
The assessments, which began October 12 and were scheduled to continue through October 29, examine the quality of education, school safety, students' psychological well-being, and their attitudes and values. They also evaluate students' ability to apply their knowledge in areas such as mathematics, science, reading and financial literacy.
The results are used to evaluate educational institutions rather than individual students and do not affect school grades or graduation eligibility.
Rosobrnadzor did not disclose how the attackers gained access to the assessment platform or whether any information was stolen.
In a statement published Saturday, Black Spark claimed that Russian schoolchildren had welcomed the disruption and sent the group numerous messages of support. The hackers, however, denied seeking to recruit minors into their activities.
"Under no circumstances does our movement recruit children into its activities, and we categorically oppose any attempts to involve minors in the war," the group said.
The group nevertheless encouraged adults to join its campaign against the Russian government.
Black Spark has previously claimed responsibility for attacks on Russian technology infrastructure. In August, the group said it had breached Russian software developer Microolap. The company acknowledged that some of its systems had been compromised but disputed the hackers' claims that they had accessed its network monitoring platform or stolen data belonging to major Russian companies.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Defense contractors in two NATO allies hacked in recent Russia-linked campaign
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The Russian group known as APT28 and Fancy Bear used a recently documented backdoor to dwell in the networks of two defense contractors and a law enforcement agency in two NATO allies, researchers said.
articles.full_text:
Defense contractors in two NATO allies hacked in recent Russia-linked campaign
Russian state-linked hackers targeted a naval shipbuilder, a military aircraft engine manufacturer and a law enforcement agency in two NATO countries in a recent espionage campaign, researchers have found.
The attacks were attributed to APT28, a hacking group linked to Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU, according to cybersecurity firm Symantec. The researchers did not identify the two NATO countries or the organizations targeted, saying only that the victims were located in Europe.
The hackers used a recently discovered backdoor known as Hookedge to gain access to victims' systems, steal credentials and gather information about their networks. The malware was first documented in August by Recorded Future's Insikt Group.
In one attack against a naval shipbuilder, the hackers gained access after an employee opened a malicious Microsoft Word document received as an email attachment in July. The attackers subsequently explored the company's internal network and attempted to steal login credentials.
Over the following week, the hackers repeatedly returned to a compromised computer and deployed a previously undocumented tool designed to decrypt and execute malicious code directly in the computer's memory. The tool's ultimate purpose remains unclear.
The first confirmed infection occurred on July 24, while related malicious activity was detected as late as September 24. The timeline suggests the operation spanned at least two months, although researchers could not establish whether the attackers maintained uninterrupted access throughout that period.
Dick O'Brien, an intelligence analyst at Symantec, told Recorded Future News that researchers could not determine whether the attackers succeeded in stealing sensitive information.
"Given the nature of the targets, it's reasonable to assume that defense-related information was the objective of the attacks," O'Brien said. "In some cases, the attackers were on the network for a few weeks, which may have given them opportunities to obtain data."
According to Symantec, the selection of targets suggests the attacks were part of a broader Russian intelligence-gathering effort focused on European government and defense organizations.
O'Brien said the continued activity observed in September, following Recorded Future's initial findings in August, suggests the espionage campaign is ongoing.
APT28, also known as Fancy Bear, BlueDelta and Forest Blizzard, has conducted cyber-espionage operations against military, government and defense organizations in Europe and North America for more than a decade. The group gained international attention in 2016 after being linked to the hacking of the Democratic National Committee ahead of the U.S. presidential election.
Western cybersecurity agencies have repeatedly warned about the group's efforts to compromise organizations involved in defense and military logistics, particularly those supporting Ukraine.
In April, British security officials warned that APT28 had exploited vulnerabilities in internet routers to redirect web traffic and spy on victims. Earlier this year, researchers also identified activity linked to the group targeting maritime, transportation and diplomatic organizations in countries including Poland, Slovenia, Turkey, Greece and the United Arab Emirates.
Last year, more than 20 Western intelligence and cybersecurity agencies issued a joint advisory accusing APT28 of targeting logistics providers and technology companies involved in delivering foreign assistance to Ukraine.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: Judge denies WhatsApp’s bid to hold spyware maker in contempt for allegedly targeting users
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: WhatsApp argued that NSO Group violated a 2025 injunction against using the messaging app to spread spyware. A federal judge said WhatsApp hurt its case by not revealing enough information.
articles.full_text:
Judge denies WhatsApp’s bid to hold spyware maker in contempt for allegedly targeting users
A Northern California federal judge ruled that WhatsApp failed to prove a prominent spyware company violated a court injunction requiring it to stop using the messaging app’s infrastructure to mount snooping attacks on customers.
The ruling Friday by Judge Phyllis Hamilton was in response to an appeal WhatsApp filed in June. The Meta-owned messaging service wanted the judge to hold the NSO Group — maker of the powerful zero-click Pegasus spyware deployed against 1,400 app users in 2019 — in contempt for what WhatsApp called spearphishing attacks against individuals.
Hamilton issued the injunction against NSO in 2025 and fined it $4.4 million, agreeing with WhatsApp that the spyware maker had improperly abused its infrastructure to target and, in some cases, infect users’ devices with spyware.
Despite winning the overall case, however, WhatsApp failed to convince Hamilton that NSO had violated the injunction because it did not provide enough “clear and convincing evidence” of the alleged misbehavior, the judge said.
“In the court’s view, plaintiffs took a calculated risk in choosing to limit the level of detail in their supporting evidence,” Hamilton’s opinion said.
WhatsApp put forward evidence that solely relied on the testimony of Andrew Blaich, a security engineer investigator on Meta’s threat intelligence team.
Blaich submitted a declaration that alleged he found 23 new Whatsapp accounts carrying
“technical and behavioral signatures that Meta has previously associated with NSO
testing, including account registration patterns, device and other related information, and
connections to known NSO-controlled infrastructure,” according to the opinion, quoting from Blaich’s declaration.
WhatsApp told Hamilton it was concerned about providing specifics about how Blaich found the activity because divulging methods could make it much harder for the tech giant to fight spyware companies in the future.
In September 2024, Apple dropped a suit against NSO because it said continuing the case risked exposing “vital security information.”
Digital freedoms advocates condemned the decision Hamilton issued Friday, saying it would be self-sabotage for WhatsApp to unveil its tracking protocols publicly.
“Judges working on spyware cases should consider in making these decisions that WhatsApp exposing its own research and detection methods could provide enormous benefits to NSO, as well as foreign intelligence services, exploit developers and criminals that can learn how sophisticated spyware is detected and how platforms operate,” Natalia Krapiva, senior tech-counsel at Access Now told Recorded Future News via text message.
Krapiva said that requiring such disclosures in order to hold NSO accountable would “lead to complete impunity for the spyware industry.”
WhatsApp and NSO Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Feds Suspect Ransom Negotiator Ran ShinyHunters Extortion Site
articles.snippet: U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
articles.full_text:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.
Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “Rey,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.
In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.
The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.
Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap. Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.
According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.
Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).
On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records. Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.
A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.
That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.
SHINYWIRE
KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “shinywire[.]com.” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.
The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.
The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.
Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor).
In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.
The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok, the former chief executive of Cypfer, a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”
Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc. He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.
GHOSTBYTE
According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte. In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma, a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.
A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com.
“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”
It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.
Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).
In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.
“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”
The statement said CyberSteward and Cypfer are separate companies with no officers, directors or employees in common, and that Cypfer was recently acquired by the Apros Group, a holding company led by Jason Hogg, a former FBI special agent and former CEO of Aon Cyber Solutions Group. In 2020, Aon aquired Cytelligence, a security consulting firm where Mr. Tobok was founder and CEO and Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner.
CONFLICTING INTERESTS
It is not illegal in the United States to pay hackers for an encryption key to unlock servers infected with ransomware, or in exchange for a promise to delete any stolen files and refrain from publishing them online. While victim organizations can land in legal hot water if they pay a ransom to a group that is sanctioned by the U.S. Treasury Department, ShinyHunters is not among the ransomware groups currently sanctioned by the United States or by any other government.
Experts say ransomware victims are typically directed by their insurance provider to work with a specific incident response firm. But not all cyber forensics and breach response companies will agree to facilitate payments to ransomware groups on behalf of their clients. As a result, once victim firms make a decision to pay, the firms that eschew rewarding extortionists are invariably replaced by companies that have no such qualms.
In December 2024, ShinyHunters began extorting the education technology company PowerSchool, stealing private information on 62 million students and 9.5 million teachers in the U.S. and Canada. PowerSchool reportedly paid a $2.85 million ransom demand, and a “frequently asked questions” statement (PDF) about the breach says PowerSchool was assisted in that effort by CyberSteward (ShinyHunters affiliate Matthew Lane, 20, of Sterling, Mass., was sentenced in November 2025 to four years in prison for his admitted role in the PowerSchool hack).
But that ransom payment did not stop future extortion attempts using the same stolen data. By May 2025, individual school districts were reportedly receiving separate ransom demands using samples of the same stolen files. While nobody has alleged ShinyHunters was behind the second wave of extortion against PowerSchool users, the incident drives home the reality that there is no technical way to verify the threat actors have deleted the stolen data as promised, or prevent others from abusing the same records.
A number of leading cyber incident response firms, including Coveware and Unit 221B, have consistently warned victims against paying ShinyHunters, noting that “destroyed” victim data is often kept, resold or used to extort the company’s clients directly later on.
The FBI echoed those sentiments in an alert on May 15, 2026 advising victims against paying the ShinyHunters group. Meanwhile, ShinyHunters members have been harassing and threatening employees at Coveware and Unit 221B for offering this advice.
The following screenshots show just how annoyed the ShinyHunters leaders were with Coveware’s relentless advice against paying the group. The first image is from a conversation on May 6, 2026 that took place between the group’s main account on Telegram and a co-conspirator. In that chat, snippets of which were shared with KrebsOnSecurity by a trusted source, ShinyHunters complained that Coveware was harming the group’s payment rates.
“Go on my website, majority of those companies would’ve paid if it weren’t for Coveware giving them misinformation,” the ShinyHunters account wrote. “Someone (100% Coveware) is going out of their way to make sure i am not paid.”
In another conversation on April 11, 2026, the ShinyHunters Telegram account privately said they were trying to “eliminate the problem,” which they said was Coveware. Coveware declined to comment for this story.
“I’m sure the company will pay but in this specific case I am aware of Coveware and their involvement, and I’ve probably been not getting a lot of other negotiations mostly likely because Coveware keeps getting involved,” the ShinyHunters account bemoaned.
Mark Camillo is chief executive at CyberAcuView, an industry group founded in 2021 by a consortium of major cyber insurance carriers. Camillo said some firms charge a flat retainer fee, while those that specialize in helping companies negotiate a ransom payment tend to charge a percentage of the total ransom amount paid.
That latter dynamic, he said, is an inherent conflict of interest, as the negotiator has every incentive to make things more favorable to the attackers because they are financially incentivized to negotiate and pay out, and to not negotiate down on the price.
“It has come to the industry’s attention that many of the ransomware payers charge a percentage of the final payment which may or may not be disclosed,” Camillo said. “This makes no sense if they are also the negotiator. There needs to be more transparency in the process as no one in the ecosystem should be profiting purely on the size of the ransomware transaction or payment itself.”
Camillo said the firms doing this work would argue the fees are needed because there may be unexpectedly higher costs to secure larger quantities of cryptocurrency or more risk carrying the float, and because cryptocurrency exchanges may charge higher fees for high risk transactions.
“There definitely needs to be more visibility around the transaction and clarity on the increasing value of the crypto and the exchange’s percent in the transaction to get to the bottom of this and remove any misaligned incentives,” he said.
In recent months, the U.S. Department of Justice has prosecuted a number of ransomware negotiators alleged to have conspired with cybercriminals to defraud their clients. On October 7, the DOJ charged MonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.snippet: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.
As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.
“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”
In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.
TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.
Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”
As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.
Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.
Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.
Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.
That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.
“Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.”

articles.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
articles.snippet: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today's epic patch batch dwarfs September's record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.
Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).
At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.
While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.
Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.
“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.
Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.
Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.
“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.
Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.
One has to wonder how big the backlog of flaws is at this point. Maybe this month’s increase in the number of fixes just reflects an increasing number of people working on these fixes, and that they already have enough flaws to keep them all busy for a long time. Oh to be a fly on the wall.
